summary: Provides examples of S/MIME messages, including Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) objects and the MIME formatting around them. The goal is to help implementers test and improve interoperability for S/MIME and other protocols that use CMS. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo is a set of worked examples of secure email. It shows the bytes of signed, encrypted and hashed messages, so that people writing mail software can check their work against the same samples.

subtitle: Worked examples of signed, encrypted and hashed mail, so that implementations can check their output against the same bytes.

tldr.problem: Implementors of S/MIME and of other protocols built on the Cryptographic Message Syntax have to get a long list of encodings exactly right, and the specification alone is hard to check against.
tldr.mechanism: The memo supplies the same sample content, keys, certificates and revocation lists, then shows the resulting message objects byte by byte: trivial objects, signed data in eleven variants, enveloped, digested and encrypted data, and two complete MIME messages.
tldr.outcome: Every example was checked by two different implementors, so a reader can compare their own output against a known-good sample rather than against prose.

today: RFC 4134 is an Informational memo published in July 2005, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It is a companion to the Cryptographic Message Syntax and S/MIME message specifications, and the memo warns that some dates in the examples are many years old and that some certificates have very long lifespans, which can cause problems in some test situations.

sections.title: Why A Collection Of Examples
sections.content:
This document collects examples of message bodies formatted with S/MIME. It shows examples of Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) objects, which is the format S/MIME messages are built from, and complete S/MIME messages including the MIME formatting around them. The stated purpose is to improve interoperability, for S/MIME and for other protocols that rely on CMS.

The examples show the structure and format of CMS message bodies as described in the Cryptographic Message Syntax document, and they are useful to implementors who use protocols that rely on CMS. Every example was checked by two different implementors, which strongly indicates, but does not assure, that the examples are correct. The memo is explicit that the examples are not a standalone explanation of how to create CMS message bodies: implementors still have to read the CMS document carefully before working from them.

It does not attempt to cover many PKIX examples, and it notes that the Data Validation and Certification Server Protocols document has examples of formats of its own. One warning applies to anyone testing with these files. The examples were created and validated over a long period by many people, so some of the dates in them are many years in the past, and some of the certificates have very long lifespans. That may cause problems in some test situations.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is a set of worked examples of secure email. It shows the bytes of signed, encrypted and hashed messages, so that people writing mail software can check their work against the same samples.

sections.title: The Cast And The Constants
sections.content:
The examples share a cast of five people. Alice creates the message bodies, Bob receives them, Carl is a certification authority, and Diane and Erica sometimes get involved. The document then fixes the data used throughout: the sample content, which is the single sentence This is some sample content., together with its MD5 and SHA-1 hashes; the private keys for Alice's DSS signing key, Alice's RSA signing key, Bob's RSA encryption key and Carl's DSS and RSA signing keys; the certificates; and the certificate revocation lists.

Most of the document is given over to those keys, certificates and revocation lists in ASN.1 form, so that a reader can reproduce the examples. The private keys are named for their use, so that AlicePrivDSSSign is the private half of Alice's DSS signing key and BobPrivRSAEncrypt is the private half of the key Bob uses for encryption. The certificates include ones issued by Carl as a root, and revocation lists signed by Carl.
sections.plainLanguage: Every example uses the same five people and the same sample sentence, so the only thing that changes from one example to the next is the structure of the message around it.

sections.title: Trivial Objects And The First Signed Messages
sections.content:
The trivial examples are the smallest CMS objects: a ContentInfo holding a Data object with the sample content, written once in BER, the general binary encoding, and once in DER, the distinguished encoding rules. The two differ only in how the octet string holding the content is split.

Signed data is the bulk of the document. The first signed example is a SignedData with no attribute certificates, signed by Alice using DSS, carrying only her certificate and no revocation list, with the message included in the eContent and no signed or unsigned attributes. The next example is the same thing with an RSA signature instead. A third version signs the same content but leaves the content out of the object, so that the signature is detached from the text it covers.
sections.plainLanguage: The first examples show the smallest possible message, then the same message with Alice's signature on it. One version keeps the signed text inside the message and another leaves it out.

sections.title: The Variants Of Signed Data
sections.content:
Later sections vary one thing at a time so that each feature can be seen on its own. A fancier signed object adds Carl's root certificate and Carl's revocation list, some signed attributes, which are content type, message digest and signing time, and some unsigned attributes, which are a content hint and a countersignature by Diane. A separate example shows an all-RSA signed message with Carl's root certificate but no revocation list. Another signs the same message twice, with two signerInfos, one for Alice and one for Diane, each using DSS and each carrying the signer's certificate.

Two further sections change how the signer is identified and how the result is wrapped. One uses the subject key identifier of the certificate instead of the issuer and serial number. Two sections then give complete S/MIME messages, including the MIME headers: one as a multipart/signed message with the signed text in the first part and a base64 signature part named smime.p7s, and one as a single application/pkcs7-mime part with the whole signed object base64 encoded in a file named smime.p7m.

The last two signed-data sections cover attributes and certificates alone. The attributes example lists eight signed attributes: an unknown object identifier, content hints, S/MIME capabilities, a security label, a content reference, S/MIME encrypt key preference, an expansion history, and an equivalent label. The certificates-only example is a signed object with no content and no signature at all, carrying only Alice's certificate and Carl's.
sections.plainLanguage: Each later example changes one thing: adding certificates, adding attributes, signing with two people, or wrapping the signature in mail headers. That way each feature can be checked on its own.

sections.title: Enveloped, Digested And Encrypted Data
sections.content:
The enveloped-data examples show a message encrypted for Bob with the content key managed by RSA. The first uses TripleDES in CBC mode for the content, with an 8-byte initialisation vector, and the second uses RC2 with a 128-bit key. Neither carries an OriginatorInfo. A third section gives the complete S/MIME message, an application/pkcs7-mime part with the type enveloped-data and the encrypted object base64 encoded in a file named smime.p7m.

The digested-data example is a hash of the sample content using SHA-1, with the hash value included alongside the content. The two encrypted-data examples differ from enveloped data in that the encrypted bytes are wrapped directly: a simple EncryptedData with no attributes, and an EncryptedData with unprotected attributes, where the protected content is encrypted with TripleDES in CBC mode and an unprotected attribute carries a short test string under the object identifier 1 2 5555.
sections.plainLanguage: The encrypted examples show the two ways mail software can hide a message: enveloped data, where a content key is wrapped for the recipient, and encrypted data, where the bytes are encrypted directly. One example shows a plain SHA-1 hash of the content.

sections.title: Security Considerations And The Extractor
sections.content:
Because the document shows S/MIME and CMS messages, it inherits all of the security considerations from the S/MIME message specification and from the Cryptographic Message Syntax document. It adds one warning of its own: the Perl script in the appendix writes to the user's local hard drive, so an attacker who could modify that script might cause harm. Readers are told to read the Perl code carefully before running it.

The appendix explains how the binary examples are stored. They are kept in a modified Base64 form in the document, in lines that begin with a pipe character. The extractor script treats a line that begins with a pipe and an asterisk as a comment, a pipe and a greater-than sign as the start of a new file, a pipe and a less-than sign as the end of a file, and anything else as Base64 data. The script writes out a series of files, so it should be run in an empty directory. It overwrites files if it can, but it does not delete other files already there.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds no new security rules of its own. It does warn that the script that unpacks the example files writes to your disk, so read it before you run it.

items.title: DSS and RSA
items.text: The same basic signed content, signed once with DSS and once with RSA.

items.title: Detached content
items.text: The signature is present but the signed text is not included in the object.

items.title: Certificates and CRLs
items.text: Some variants add Carl's root certificate and his revocation list.

items.title: Attributes
items.text: Signed attributes are covered by the signature; unsigned attributes such as a countersignature are not.

items.title: Multiple signers
items.text: Two signerInfos, one for Alice and one for Diane.

items.title: Subject key identifier
items.text: One variant identifies the signer by subject key identifier instead of issuer and serial number.

items.title: Certificates only
items.text: A signed object with no content and no signature, carrying only certificates.
